name: Public humiliation
definition: A public act or remark, by an identifiable author, that belittles or ridicules the followed player by name.
inclusionCriteria: The act or remark targets the player by name; it belittles him (mockery, contempt, doubt cast on his worth or status, a derisive gesture); its author is identifiable by role (opponent, coach, his own included, executive, media outlet, commentator); it is reported by at least one dated press article.
exclusionCriteria: Criticism of a specific play in an ordinary game analysis; an anonymous social-media message the press does not report; a play suffered on the court, unless an identified author then mocks it publicly; racist remarks (type "Racist abuse"); a hostile exchange between the player and another player (type "Conflict between players"); a wave of criticism from several outlets with no single triggering remark (type "Media storm").
datingRule: The moment the remark or act becomes public (live broadcast, publication), established by the first dated article that reports it.
genericExample: The day before a game, the coach of team X says at a press conference that player A is not at the level of a top player; a national outlet reports it that evening; the measured game is player A's game the next day.
cautionNotes: The line between this and ordinary criticism is the most delicate of the list; the criterion "targets the player's worth, not a specific play" must be tried on a few real articles before validation.

name: Racist abuse
definition: The followed player is the target of racist remarks, gestures or messages reported by the press.
inclusionCriteria: The press reports that the player was personally targeted; the author is designated by role (spectator, opponent, public figure, author of online messages); the incident is dated.
exclusionCriteria: A general racist climate with no incident targeting the player; the player speaking about racism in general, with no incident targeting him; an incident targeting another player.
datingRule: If the incident happened during a game, it is public from that moment, and the measured game is the next game; otherwise the date is that of the first dated article that reports it.
genericExample: During an away game, a spectator shouts racist insults at player A; a national outlet reports it the next day; the measured game is player A's next game.
cautionNotes: Intimate-subject mark; the description follows the sensitive-data rules (never the terms used, the author designated by role); only incidents the press reported can be found.

name: Player's birthday
definition: The followed player plays a game on his birthday.
inclusionCriteria: An official NBA game of his team falls on his birthday.
exclusionCriteria: A birthday with no game that day; the birthday of a loved one; the anniversary of another event (title, death, record).
datingRule: Known in advance and derived from the calendar: the reference date is the birthday itself, before tip-off, and the measured game is that day's game.
genericExample: Player A turns thirty on the day of a game against team X; several outlets mention it that morning.
cautionNotes: Clean and datable by nature; its fact is read from the schedule rather than the press, which sets it apart from the other types.

name: Approaching a positive historic record
definition: The press presents the followed player as able to equal or break a notable record in his next game.
inclusionCriteria: A dated article, published before the game, presents the record as within reach in that game; the record is individual (a league record, a record of his team's history, or a career milestone the press presents as historic).
exclusionCriteria: A team record; a record already broken; a statistical curiosity no outlet presents before the game; the following games, when the record is not broken in the first game presented as decisive, because a record gives only one event.
datingRule: The first publication that presents the record as within reach in the next game.
genericExample: The day before a game, a national outlet writes that player A is only a few points short of the scoring record of team X's history.
cautionNotes: The team may steer play toward the player to help him break the record, which inflates his performance index for reasons unrelated to ego; the event is defined by the approach, known before the game, never by the record being broken.

name: Negative record to avoid
definition: The press presents the followed player as exposed, in his next game, to a notable negative outcome or record that he can still avoid.
inclusionCriteria: A dated article, published before the game, presents that game as the one where the negative outcome can happen, for example elimination by a sweep after trailing 3-0 in a series, a record losing streak or a negative personal record; the article names the player, not only his team.
exclusionCriteria: A situation presented as the team's without the player being named; a negative record already suffered; a threat mentioned only after the game.
datingRule: The first publication that presents the next game as the one where the negative outcome can happen.
genericExample: Player A's team X trails 3-0 in a playoff series; before game 4, a national outlet headlines the risk that player A suffers his first series sweep.
cautionNotes: This type overlaps by construction with a high-stakes game, a known confounder; if an elimination game's unusual stakes are enough to exclude a case, almost all its cases will be excluded, unless the unusual-stakes criterion is switched off for the type; the boundary with a team event rests entirely on the criterion "the player is named".

name: Death of a loved one
definition: The death of a loved one of the followed player is made public.
inclusionCriteria: The press reports the death of a member of the player's family or of a person it presents as close to him; the news is dated.
exclusionCriteria: The death of a public figure with no personal tie to the player established by the press; the anniversary of a death; a loved one's illness.
datingRule: The moment the death becomes public, that is its announcement, not the date of death if earlier.
genericExample: A national outlet announces the death of a loved one of player A two days before a game; player A plays that game.
cautionNotes: Intimate-subject mark; the description gives no name, family relationship or cause; the player may miss games, and his measured game is then the game of his return.

name: Conflict between players
definition: A public clash, verbal or physical, between the followed player and another player, opponent or teammate.
inclusionCriteria: The player is one of the parties; the clash is public (an altercation during a game, an exchange of statements, a dispute made public); it is reported by a dated article.
exclusionCriteria: A one-sided attack the player suffers without answering (type "Public humiliation"); the ordinary verbal exchanges of a game, which the press does not present as a conflict; a dispute with a coach or an executive (type "Public humiliation" if it belittles the player, no type otherwise).
datingRule: The moment the conflict becomes public: during the game where it breaks out, the measured game then being the next one; otherwise, the first publication.
genericExample: At the end of a game, player A and a player of team X shout at each other; several outlets report the exchange; the measured game is player A's next game, whoever the opponent.
cautionNotes: A suspension may follow a physical conflict, and the measured game is then the game of his return; if both players are followed, the conflict gives one event for each.

name: Media storm
definition: A wave of negative coverage centered on the followed player, triggered by an identifiable public fact: a statement, a behavior, a controversy about his commitment.
inclusionCriteria: A public, dated triggering fact; critical articles from at least three distinct outlets within two days (the sheet's coverage threshold); the player is at the center of the coverage.
exclusionCriteria: An isolated critical remark (type "Public humiliation"); a conflict with another player (type "Conflict between players"); a racist incident (type "Racist abuse"); a controversy touching the player's private life or health.
datingRule: The moment the coverage threshold is reached, that is the publication of the article that crosses it; one triggering fact gives only one event.
genericExample: After a statement by player A judged offhand, three national outlets publish critical articles about his commitment within two days; the measured game is player A's first game after the third article.
cautionNotes: The least clean type of the list, whose dating depends on a threshold; it is hard to reconstruct afterwards, so a backtest will mostly find the storms that stayed famous, often because a striking answer on the court followed.

name: Game against a former team
definition: The followed player faces, for the first time since leaving it, an NBA team he played for.
inclusionCriteria: An official NBA game; the player played at least one official game for the opposing team; it is their first meeting since his departure.
exclusionCriteria: Preseason or exhibition games; former teams outside the NBA; a team for which he played no official game.
datingRule: Known in advance and derived from the calendar: the reference date is the game's day, before tip-off, so that the measured game is that game itself.
genericExample: Traded by team X during the summer, player A faces it for the first time in November; several outlets present the game as his reunion with team X.
cautionNotes: Like the birthday, this type is known in advance and read from the schedule rather than the press; its measured game is the event itself.
